name: David Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and what you tell me is confidential. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a patrol officer on the north side of the city, the suburbs past the ring road, where it's houses, a retail park and a lot of traffic. We do rotating shifts, two days, two lates, two nights. A lot of my calls are collisions on Mill Road, shoplifting at the retail park and domestic calls in the estates behind it. Six years in now, so I know the area and a fair few of the families.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what gets on your nerves?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy knowing the patch: which junction floods, which shopkeeper will actually give a statement. What gets on my nerves is every new system they bring in, because each one means another login and another training afternoon. I don't use AI, not at work and not at home. My girlfriend Ama uses it to plan holidays, and I let her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: told you so. Every year there's some new thing that's going to change policing, and every year I'm still on Mill Road at three in the morning measuring skid marks. I wouldn't post anything, I'm not really online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing much changes for me, and I'm happy with that. The job's steady, the pay's fair, and I've got about three months put by. My worries are normal ones, like whether Ama and I can afford a flat of our own in the next couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, really. Keep doing my shifts and keep saving the 250 a month we put away for a deposit. If the force makes me use some AI form-filler, I'll go to the training and use it as little as I can get away with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Relieved, if anything. I like things that stay where you left them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use the tool as little as you can. Why hold back if it saves time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when I write a report myself, I remember the job. If a machine writes it and I just sign, I'll be standing in court in a year with no idea what happened. I'd rather spend the extra twenty minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the flat mean for you and Ama?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've been renting off her cousin for two years, and it's fine, but it's not ours. I'd like a place with a parking space so I'm not hunting for one after a night shift. In this picture we get there, just slowly.

say: I'd say **told you so**: every year something is meant to change policing.
I wouldn't post anything; I'm **not really online**.
think: Nothing much changes, and I'm **happy** with a steady job and fair pay.
My real worry is affording a **flat** with Ama in the next couple of years.
do: Keep working my **rotating shifts** on the north side.
Keep saving **250 a month** towards a flat deposit.
Use any AI form-filler **as little** as I can.
feel: **Relieved**; he likes things that stay where he left them.
S0.quote: When I write a report myself, I remember the job.
fieldNote: He distrusts AI reports because of **court**: he needs to remember what he saw.
His real pressure is **housing**, not technology.
He takes comfort in **routine** and names local streets with clear affection.

steps.text: Keep working rotating patrol shifts on the north side
Keep putting 250 a month towards a flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd grumble along with everyone else, probably louder. I'd say, fine, let the computer answer the non-emergency line, but someone still has to turn up. To friends I'd say my job's one of the safe ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be less sure. If the software writes the reports and plans the shifts, then the bosses will say one officer can cover what two did. They wouldn't sack anyone, but they'd stop hiring and squeeze overtime, and overtime is how we're saving for the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new system because I'd have to, but only the bits I need. I'd cut the takeaway nights and the football away trips so the deposit fund doesn't stall if overtime dries up. Mostly I'd wait and see what the force actually does before I change anything big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Irritated more than scared. Like being told to change a habit that works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your pay is overtime, roughly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year maybe a sixth of it, mostly from covering nights when people were off sick. If the overtime goes, the 250 a month we save for a flat becomes about 150. That's another year before we've got a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work you'd worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bev in the control room. She's been taking 999 calls for fifteen years and she's brilliant, but she's exactly what they'd try to replace with a computer. Bev (a call handler at his station) would be the first one I'd ring if I heard about cuts.

say: I'd say someone still has to **turn up**, whatever the computer does.
I'd tell friends policing is one of the **safe jobs**.
think: The bosses would **stop hiring** and expect one officer to do two people's work.
Losing **overtime** would slow our saving for the flat.
do: Learn only the parts of the **new system** I need.
Cut takeaways and **away trips** to protect the deposit fund.
**Wait and see** what the force does before any big change.
feel: **Irritated** at being made to change a habit that works.
S1.quote: If the overtime goes, the 250 a month we save for a flat becomes about 150.
fieldNote: His public line of **safety** hides a private fear about **overtime**.
He reads the threat as **squeezed hours**, not lost jobs, which fits a pragmatic outlook.
He thinks first of a **call handler** colleague, not himself.

steps.text: Cut takeaway nights and away football trips
Hold off on big changes until the force announces plans
Learn only the parts of the new report system he needs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think I'd say much in public, to be honest. I'd tell the lads it's nonsense until it isn't. If the Police Federation called a meeting, I'd go, which I've never done before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it frightens me. Two years is nothing. If a computer can do the thinking by 2028, then the reports, the statements, the case files, even deciding who gets sent where, all go to it. That leaves me as the bloke in the car. By 2031 a robot can be the bloke in the car, and I'd be 31 with no other trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything that isn't rent and food, straight away. Ama and I would put the flat on hold, because I'm not signing a mortgage on a job that might not exist. I'd go to the Federation meetings and back anything that protects officers' jobs. And I'd ask my uncle Kofi about his plumbing business, which I've never wanted to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like the floor's moving and I can't see where it stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ama the night you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we're not buying the flat this year, and probably not next year either. She'd say we'll be fine because her job is in people's mouths, not on a screen. Ama (his girlfriend) is a dental hygienist, and she'd probably be right for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your uncle's plumbing business. Why does that come up now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because plumbing is hands-on and robots come later. My uncle Kofi has asked me twice to come and learn the trade, and I laughed both times. In this picture I'd stop laughing.

say: I'd tell the lads it's **nonsense** until it isn't.
I'd go to my first **Police Federation** meeting and back it.
I'd keep my real fear off social media and away from **the station**.
think: Two years is **nothing**; reports, files and dispatch go to the computer.
By 2031 robots could replace the **bloke in the car**, and I'd have no other trade.
do: Cut spending to **rent and food** straight away.
Put the **flat purchase** on hold with Ama.
Ask uncle Kofi about learning **plumbing** in his business.
feel: **Sick**, like the floor is moving and won't stop.
S2.quote: By 2031 a robot can be the bloke in the car, and I'd be 31 with no other trade.
fieldNote: The fast timeline breaks his usual **wait and see** stance completely.
He swings to a **trade** he'd mocked, showing how deep the fear is.
His partner's **hands-on job** is the household's anchor in his telling.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent, bills and food straight away
Put the plan to buy a flat with Ama on hold
Attend Police Federation meetings and back job protection
Ask uncle Kofi to start teaching him plumbing at weekends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the fast one, I'd keep it quiet in public. Maybe I'd tell people at five-a-side that there's still time. I'd say the force will need people for a while yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is better, but it's still close. I'd be 32 when the computers take the desk side and about 35 when robots come for the street side. That's still young enough to learn something, but I'd be starting at the bottom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving, maybe bump the deposit savings up to 300. I'd do my uncle Kofi's plumbing on some weekends from the second year, just to see if I like it. I'd still hold off on the flat for a year or two until I could see what the force does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a knot in my stomach. Not panicked, but not sleeping great either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd start at the bottom. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An apprentice wage at 35, taking orders from a nineteen-year-old who's better at it than me. That's the bit I'd hate. Policing gave me respect quite young, and I'd be giving that up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you watch for in those five years to decide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the force stops recruiting. When they stop taking new officers, that's the sign. My cousin's a recruiter for the force, so I'd hear about it early.

say: I'd tell the five-a-side lot there's still **time**.
I'd say the force will **need people** for a while yet.
think: Five years is better but still **close**: 32 for desk work, 35 for robots.
Starting a new trade means **starting at the bottom**.
do: Raise deposit savings to **300 a month**.
Try **weekend plumbing** with uncle Kofi from the second year.
Delay the **flat** until the force's plans are clear.
feel: **Uneasy** with a knot in his stomach, and not sleeping great.
S3.quote: Policing gave me respect quite young, and I'd be giving that up.
fieldNote: The loss he fears most is **status**, not only income.
He has a clear **warning sign**: the force stopping recruitment.
He would test a new trade **slowly**, which fits his resistant style.

steps.text: Raise deposit savings from 250 to 300 a month
Do weekend plumbing jobs with uncle Kofi from the second year
Watch for the force freezing recruitment before buying a flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is ages, let's see. People said self-driving cars would be everywhere by now, and I'm still pulling crashed ones out of hedges. I'd say it with a laugh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is about what I'd want. I'd be 37 when AGI comes and about 40 when robots come. By then maybe I've made sergeant, or maybe I've moved over to my uncle's trade. I'd have time to make a proper choice, which is all I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd change nothing big. I'd buy the flat with Ama next year as planned, because a decade is long enough to pay a good chunk off. I'd keep the 250 a month going into savings and keep an eye on the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the back of my mind, but I'd get on with life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy the flat in this picture but not the others. What tips it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time. In ten years I can pay off a good bit of a mortgage and sell if I have to. In two years I'd be stuck with a mortgage and maybe no job. It's the same flat, different maths.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You laughed about self-driving cars. Is that what you really believe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half. I've been told so many big things that never came. But ten years is a long time, and I'm not daft. If AGI turns up in 2036, I want to have had a plan by 2033.

say: I'd say ten years is **ages**, and joke about **self-driving cars**.
I'd say big promises about technology rarely arrive **on time**.
think: Ten years gives me time to make **a proper choice**.
By 40 I might be a **sergeant** or working my uncle's trade.
do: Buy the **flat** with Ama next year as planned.
Keep saving **250 a month** and watch the news.
Make a **career plan** by 2033 if AGI still looks likely.
feel: **Uneasy** at the back of his mind, but getting on with life.
S4.quote: In ten years I can pay off a good bit of a mortgage and sell if I have to.
fieldNote: The **mortgage maths** flips with the timeline; he spelled it out clearly.
His joking **scepticism** is half real and half a way to cope.
He sets himself a quiet **deadline** of 2033 to have a plan.

steps.text: Buy a flat with a parking space with Ama next year
Keep working patrol shifts and saving 250 a month
Decide by 2033 between sergeant exams and his uncle's trade

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years isn't enough for anyone to sort anything out, least of all me. What would help is the force telling us straight what's coming, and paying for officers to learn a trade before they're let go, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who'd answer the door when a robot knocks to say someone's died. I've done that six times. Nobody should get the news that someone's died from a machine, whatever the machine can do.

headlineQuote: Nobody should get the news that someone's died from a machine, whatever the machine can do.
portrait: David is a **27-year-old patrol officer** on the city's north side, six years in, who never uses AI.
He lives with his girlfriend Ama, a **dental hygienist**, and they are saving for a flat.
In slow worlds he grumbles and **waits**; in fast AGI he cuts spending and considers **plumbing**.
His fears centre on **overtime**, status and a mortgage on a job that might vanish.
He values **routine** and local knowledge, and believes some news must come from a person.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short for anyone to adjust.
whatWouldHelp: The force being **straight** about plans, and paying for officers to **learn a trade** before job cuts.
